# Introduction #

In this report we present preliminary exploration of the LA dataset. We present different type of analysis based on the evaluation of surveillance efficacy and minimal effort needed using Sepulveda and Eldorado dataset.

# Dataset description #

## Surveillance effort ##

Starting in the late 80s, the dataset includes 161 traps of 6 types (BGSENT, CO2, GRVD, NJLT, USDS, OTHER?) accross 81 sites (trap location) in 2 areas (Sepulveda and Eldorado).
Figure \@ref(fig:ActiveSurveillance) shows, until 2004 only 3 traps NJLT type were set up (2 in Sepulva and 1 in Eldorado). Then, we observe lot of variation in the number of trap set up.  
- All trap do not have the same number of monitor weeks.  
- Increase of monitoring after 2003 related to **WNV first detection in California in 2003** [@reisen_west_2004].  
- Since 2010 decrease of monitoring effort (Figrue \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear). 

```{r ActiveSurveillance, fig.cap="Active surveillance by trap (1 trap is 1 trap type and 1 location) per week in Eldorado (top) and Sepulveda (bottom). Each blue line represents a week during which the trap was active", out.width="80%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/B - ActiveSurveillance.png")

```


### Surveillance effort over years ###
Surveillance efforts varies over years and areas (Figure \@ref(fig:ActiveWeekSurveillance)). Higher effort of surveillance occurs around 2005 and then decrease. Early season monitoring decrease a lot after 2011 with almost no trap before midmay for last years. From 2005, the number of weeks monitor is higher in Sepulveda than in El Dorado.

```{r ActiveWeekSurveillance, fig.cap="Number of weeks with at least one active trap all year around (top), for early season from january to mid may (middle), for late season after mid october (bottom), over monitored weeks", out.width="60%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/B - ActiveWeekSurveillance.png")

```

Trap_ID = one location and one type of trap.

Figure  \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear) shows that the number of trap (one location, one type of trap) at least set up once a year each year vary a lot with an high increase after 2004. Some trap have been set up for years, other as been set up sporadically (Figure \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear)).

```{r NtrapsYear, fig.cap="Number of trap set up at least once by year (right) and Number of weeks monitored by each trap (left).",  out.width="45%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center", fig.show="hold", fig.layout="column"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/D - Histogram ntraps by year for selection.png")
knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/D - Histogram traps X nweeks for selection.png")

```


### Surveillance effort by trap type ###

The different type of trap are not used consistently (Figure \@ref(fig:TrappingEffort)). NJLT had been set up in only 3 locations, but was the only trap used until 2004 and so tthe trap with the highest effort (number of trap-nights). 
After 2004, CO2 and GRVD trap was the main trap used in many different location. USDS and BGSENT are used sporadically.

```{r TrappingEffort, fig.cap="Trapping effort by type of Trap with number of location by trap type (left), number of weeks recorded by trap type (middle) and the total number of trap nights by trap type (right)", out.width="50%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Trapping effort.png")

```


## Mosquito Diversity ##

19 different species has been identified with *Cx. quiquefasciatus* represent 93% of the total sample mosquitoes (Figure \@ref(fig:HistogramSpecies)).

```{r HistogramSpecies, fig.cap="Proportion of moquitoes species from 1988 to 2022", out.width="50%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Histogram.png")

```

  
## Type of trap impact on species ##

Trap performance to capture mosquitoes vary depending on species.
Concerning the *Cx. quinquefasciatus* (except other) only NJLT capture less *Cx. quinquefasciatus* than average. NJLT trap is less efficient to capture *Cx. quiquefasciatus* [@reisen_comparative_1999]. 
According to the figure it seems that we get the general trend with only CO2 and NJLT trap (except for *Ae. notoscriptus* capture only once).
"Other" type trap only catch *Ae. aegypti* is it Human-landing catch ? 
Figure \@ref(fig:CorrespondenceTable) show that long old series NJLT trap do not capture a lot of Cx. quiquefasciatus. 

```{r CorrespondenceTable, fig.cap="Detection of mosquito species by trap type", out.width="80%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Correspondence table.png")

```

# Surveillance efficacy.  

**Due to a significant change in the monitoring method and the use of only one trap type before 2004, the rest of the analysis will use only data from 2004 to 2022 (Figure  \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear))**.  
Different methods can be used to evaluate surveillance efficacy. To do so we need first to choose indacator on which we will evaluate the performance. We drew inspiration from a study in New Orleans who has been evaluating different types of traps for monitoring mosquitoes over several years [@scavo_mosquito_2026]. 
- Shanon : alpha diversity. 
- Culex quinqufasciatus dynamic : general trend, start season, end season. 
- Aedes aegypti : delay in first detection. 

MC indicators

To estimate the importance of each trap (indivually and by trap type) we used the Shapley value. It come from game theory and allow to compute each player (trap) contribution to the outcome (performance). It calculates each player's average marginal contribution across all possible coalitions. 
Here we present a Monte Carlo adpted version of it (otherwise, it would take way too long) with 10000 permutations.


## Impact on alpha diversity (Shanon). 

### Impact of number of trap on alpha diversity (MC indicators).

```

# Perspetives / question :

- Is it possible do get a update of the data until end of 2025 ? or up to date ?

- Do we observe same tendancy in different location (same results with a different dataset)? 

- Before 2004 surveillance was very different using only one type of trap NJLT. I found in [@reisen_comparative_1999] : *"Originally, light traps were deployed to monitor Cx. tarsalis abundance in relation to enzootic virus transmission activity"*. What can we do with data before 2004 ? 

-  Performance index and species of interest : so far, we focus on Shanon diversity index, *Cx quiquefasciatus* dynamic and *Ae. aedypti* detection 
We need to discuss species of interest and performance index that can be used. We can think of eveness for example.

- Adding spatial information, we can explore the impact of the trap location.

- Urban green space and vectors : we need adidional data to do so. In previous meeting we discuss about data from two additional site : Harbor Lake – Control/ Non-Green (NEW) and Valley Urban – Control/Non-Green
